00.1 · Read this firstWhat this pack is, and what it is not

A design pack is not a description of a shop. It is a transfer of decision rights and liability from the people who designed it to the person standing in the unit with a drill.

The test every page had to pass

If a line does not change what someone does on site, or does not tell someone what to expect from the money they are about to spend, it was cut. That is why this document contains schedules, values and hold points rather than mood boards and adjectives.

Three readers, one document

ReaderWhat they need from itWhere they start
The fitterWhat stands where, what it is made of, what tolerance it is fixed at, and which sample to submit before touching anything.§03 setting out, then §06 materials, then §07 details
The franchiseeWhat they are buying, what it will cost them to own, and which decisions are theirs rather than the brand's.§01 the store, then §05 colourway, then §11 risk
The auditorWhether what is built matches what was approved, and against which document revision.§02 authority, then §10 approvals, then the annexure

Discipline

Every number in this pack is traceable to a source in the register at §02.2 — a calculation, a drawing, a brand rule, or a ruling by the principal. Where a number is authored by this pack rather than inherited, the page says so.

PP-SDP-001 · Shop Design Pack 00 · The rule

00.2 · Two documentsThe standard and the annexure

The design is issued as two documents that are generated from one colour record. The main pack never changes per store. The annexure never contains a rule.

DocumentCarriesVariesPages
PP-SDP-001
main pack		The standard: geometry, materials, lighting, details, the colourway menu, and every rule the network holds.No. One revision for all stores.61
PP-CWA-0XX
annexure		One store's colour only: plate, surface map, RGB recipe, procurement card, signage variant, three signatures.Yes. One per territory.8

Why two, and not one with a colour page stuck in the back

A standard that is edited per store stops being a standard within about eighteen months. But a standard that ignores the store's colour is a document nobody opens. Splitting them means the 61 pages are revised once, centrally, and only the 8-page annexure is reissued for each new territory. This is what makes the fiftieth store as cheap to document as the second.

The rule that holds it together

Both documents are printed from one colour record per store. The plate on the annexure and the procurement card in the same annexure cannot disagree, because neither is typed twice. A colour that exists in two places is a colour that will eventually exist in two versions.

Precedence if the two ever conflict

The main pack governs. The annexure may only narrow it for one store — never widen it, and never introduce a colour the network does not own. If an annexure is found contradicting the pack, the annexure is withdrawn and reissued; the pack is not edited to match.

Section one

The store,
and the test
it must pass

Eight by five and a half metres of shell, a food court, and one shot at a first impression. This section fixes the room, the four ways it will be judged, and the single distinction that decides every other page: what is brand and what is the store.

01.1 The room · 01.2 The four tests · 01.3 Fixed and variable · 01.4 The store as designed · 01.5 Two views of the same decision

Section 01 Issue 01 · 2026-10-20 ·  06 / 61

01.1The room

A single rectangular tenancy in a mall food court: 8 040 mm × 5 600 mm inside the shopfront line, with a 3 600 mm ceiling datum and one customer entrance. Everything in this pack is set out from those three facts.

DimensionValueNote
Internal shell8 040 × 5 600 mmInside face to inside face. Verify on site before fabrication — see §03.5.
Ceiling datum3 600 mmFinished floor to underside of ceiling. Services zone sits above it.
Floor area45.0 m²8.04 × 5.60. The number every load calculation divides by.
Shopfront8 040 mmLandlord-owned. No tenant fixings without consent — §07.4.
Customer entrance1Food court side. Circulation from it is set out at §03.2.
Staff entrance1Back of house. Never used for deliveries during trading.

Verify, do not assume

The shell dimensions come from the drawing set, not from a site survey. A shell that is 40 mm out moves every counter and every tile joint. Hold point H1 at §09.2 requires a physical survey before any fabrication order.

What the room is for

Three activities, in a fixed sequence, and the plan is only correct if all three work at the same time: a customer walks in and reads the menu, a customer orders and pays, and a customer watches pasta being cooked while they wait. Everything else — retail display, collection, back of house — is support for that 90-second loop.

The room Issue 01 · 2026-10-20 ·  07 / 61
PP-SDP-001 · Shop Design Pack 01 · The store

01.2The four tests

A store can pass a photoshoot and fail a Tuesday. These are the four tests this pack is built to satisfy, in the order they will actually be applied.

Test 1 — The fitter's test: can it be built without a phone call?

Every junction in the pack is drawn layer by layer, from substrate outward, with the fixing, the tolerance and the access route for maintenance. If a fitter has to invent a detail, the pack has failed at that point and the defect is the pack's, not theirs.

Test 2 — The franchisee's test: can the money be trusted?

What is fixed and paid once, what is chosen and paid once, and what can be changed later for the price of an afternoon instead of a closure. That distinction is the commercial heart of §05, and it is the difference between a colour you can change and a colour you are stuck with.

Test 3 — The audit test: will it still be right in three years?

A store is inspected against a document, not against a memory. Every value here is printed with the revision that governs it, so a store built in 2029 can be judged against the rules that existed when it was approved rather than the ones that exist when it is inspected.

Test 4 — The 23:00 test: is it the brightest thing on the street?

The store is white and lit at 6 000 K. At night that makes it a lit box in a food court of darker neighbours — legible from fifty metres, and noticeably harder to walk past than a black shopfront with a small logo on it. This is a deliberate consequence of the white ruling and it is why the light-trespass line in §10.1 exists.

The four tests Issue 01 · 2026-10-20 ·  08 / 61

01.3What is fixed, what is chosen, what is weekly

The single most useful distinction in this pack, and the one most often blurred: the brand is black, the shop is white, and the colour in between belongs to the store.

LayerWhat it coversWhose decisionVaries
FoundationThe 70 / 18 / 12 proportion, the type system, the crest anatomy, EST 2025, the audit rules, the product lawThe brand. Fixed forever.No
ColourwayThe store's accent colour, on the 12% and on the façade sign field. One colour per storeThe store, from the network menuYes
SignalWeekly and seasonal messages: menu boards, campaign panels, window graphicsMarketing, centrally issuedWeekly

Why the proportion inverts, and why that is not a contradiction

On a page, black is the field: 70% black, 18% white knockout, 12% accent. The brand is read, and black is what makes lime and the crest legible at a glance.

In a room, white is the field — for a physical reason, not a stylistic one. White surfaces return most of the light that hits them; black surfaces return almost none. In a store whose colour is delivered by light, that difference decides whether the colourway reads at half the installed load or looks muddy at full load. White is what makes the colour promise affordable. Same proportion, opposite polarity, one rule.

The inversion, in one line

Brand: black 70 / white 18 / accent 12.   Store: white 70 / black 18 / colour 12. The discipline is identical. Only the field changes.

02.1Who wins

Five ranks, applied in order. A lower rank may add detail; it may never contradict a higher one without a recorded variance.

#AuthorityGovernsEvidence of authority
1Ricardo Maio
principal		Network direction, money, legal, and any tie between the ranks below. The final word on what the brand will and will not do.Written rulings, 2026-10-20

The tie-breaker, stated once

Where Ryan's lighting and the Brand Manual's lighting law disagree, Ryan governs and the manual is varied in writing. The variance is recorded at §04.4 with its reason, its date and its owner — because a variance that is written down is a decision, and the same variance left unwritten is a defect found at audit.

What this hierarchy does not mean

It does not mean the lower ranks are advisory. Julie's geometry is mandatory — it simply yields to a lighting instruction that changes it, and when it does, the change is recorded here rather than silently drawn. Rank orders who wins an argument, not who matters.

03.1Shell and datum

One origin, one grid, one direction of measurement. Every subsequent dimension in this pack is expressed from it, so that a dispute is an arithmetic argument rather than a walk around the unit pointing at things.

The origin

Setting out begins at the inside face of the left-hand wall as seen from the mall, at the inside face of the shopfront line. That point is X0, Y0. X runs to the right along the shopfront; Y runs into the depth of the unit. The finished floor is Z0; the ceiling datum is Z3600.

ReferenceDefinitionValue
X0Inside face of left wall, at shopfront line0 mm
X maxInside face of right wall8 040 mm
Y0Inside face of shopfront line0 mm
Y maxInside face of rear wall5 600 mm
Z0Finished floor level0 mm
Z3600Underside of ceiling / datum for all suspended elements3 600 mm

The rule for every dimension that follows

The grid is the pack's; the dimensions are the designer's. Where a dimension is needed for fabrication it is taken from drawing A101 or A102 at 1:25 and recorded on the setting-out schedule before an order is placed. This pack does not invent a millimetre it did not receive.

What "finishes" means here

All dimensions are to finished faces — finished floor, finished wall, finished ceiling — not to structure. A fitter setting out to slab and then adding 18 mm of build-up will be 18 mm wrong on every wall, and the error compounds at every junction in the unit.

03.2Territories and circulation

A lighting zone cannot be sold and a territory cannot be lit. The pack therefore names what a franchisee can own and operate, and keeps the lighting zones as a separate language that only the lighting section speaks.

CodeTerritoryWhat happens thereCustomer / staff
CT-ENTRY-01ThresholdFirst read of the menu, first impression, the decision to walk inCustomer
CT-ORDER-02Order and payTill, under-counter refrigeration, the transactionCustomer
CT-RETAIL-03RetailDry pasta, sauces, take-home range, the display wallCustomer
CT-PASS-04The passPasta cooking, sauce, assembly, handover to the counterStaff
CT-COLLECT-05CollectPick-up, tray, condiments, the last thing a customer touchesCustomer
CT-BOH-06Back of housePrep, wash-up, storage, staff entrance, waste routeStaff

The circulation rule

There is exactly one customer path and it does not cross the staff path at any point. A customer enters, reads, orders, pays, steps aside, collects, and leaves. A staff member works the pass and never crosses the customer side except to hand over the order.

This is a food-safety requirement and a service requirement at the same time: the crossing point is where a tray gets knocked and where a health inspector writes a finding.

Why territories exist at all

Because the colourway is sold by territory (see the annexure), the lighting is designed by zone, and the fit-out is priced by area. Three languages for one room is how a schedule and a drawing drift apart. Territories are the common denominator: every zone maps to one, and every annexure page names one.

Two entries the source did not close

Z06 has no calculation. The seating area — where the customer eats the thing they bought — was never modelled. The pack specifies a level for it at §04.5 and labels it authored, not calculated.

Z03 is not named in the report's area list. The pack assigns it to the threshold and order approach as the only unallocated territory with a luminaire over it. ACDC should confirm on revision; until then the assignment governs.

Why this page matters more than it looks

Without it, a fitter installs fourteen fittings into eight areas by eye, a commissioning agent measures the wrong square metre, and the audit finds a store that is "lit to 500 lux" on average and pitch dark at the collection point. The crosswalk is what turns a lighting design into a lighting instruction.

03.5Set-out schedule and tolerances

The order of setting out is not negotiable: floor datum, then the counter line, then the walls, then the ceiling grid. Reverse it and every junction ends up packed out with silicone.

#Set outFromSource
1Finished floor datumLandlord's datum pin; verify fall to drain across the whole unit before any screedSite survey · H1

3Walls and returnsPerpendicular to the counter line, not to the shell. A shell that is out of square must not tilt the counterPack
4Tile setting-outCentre the run on the pass opening so cuts land at the least visible end; no cut under 60 mmPack · §07.3
5Ceiling grid and channelsAligned to the counter line; linear luminaires run parallel to it, not to the shellACDC + pack

Tolerances — the numbers a fitter is entitled to work to

ElementToleranceChecked with
Finished floor level, over 3 m± 3 mmStraight edge and feeler
Wall verticality, over 3 m± 3 mmSpirit level or laser
Counter top level, over length± 2 mmLaser and rule
Shadow gap, carcass to wall6 mm ± 1 mmGap gauge, at three points

Tolerances are cumulative, not additive: a wall 3 mm out and a ceiling grid 3 mm out in the same direction produces a 6 mm error at a junction that no one will accept. Set out from the counter line each time rather than from the previous trade's work.

04.1 The ruling · 04.2 Levels · 04.3 The schedule · 04.4 The variance · 04.5 The two gaps · 04.6 Quality floor and commissioning

Section 04 Issue 01 · 2026-10-20 ·  23 / 61
PP-SDP-001 · Shop Design Pack 04 · Lighting

04.1Lighting is Ryan's, in full

Twenty fittings, 698 watts, one colour temperature. This is the design that will be installed on this store and on every store after it, and the brand's own lighting law is varied to accommodate it.

Ruling 2 · 2026-10-20

Lighting is governed by Ryan Jones-Hockley / ACDC in full — levels, uniformity, colour temperature including 6 000 K, luminaire choice, quantities and wall-washing. Where the Brand Manual's lighting law disagrees, the manual is varied in writing at §04.4 rather than quietly ignored.

What that means in practice, on site

  • No substitutions without ACDC. A "same specification" fitting from a different manufacturer is a different distribution, a different colour and a different result. The schedule at §04.3 is the order.
  • No dimming to taste. Scenes are set at commissioning from the pack's scene library (§05.5). A store that dims by eye cannot be audited or supported remotely.
  • No added decorative fixtures without a written variation, because every extra fitting changes the power density, the scene balance and the colour rendering in the room.

Why 6 000 K is the right base — a design argument, not a preference

A neutral white is the only base on which a chosen colour reads as itself. Warm light tints every blue towards grey-green and every lime towards yellow, so a store lit at 2 700 K does not show the colour the franchisee chose — it shows an approximation of it. At 6 000 K the white surfaces stay neutral and the RGB wash lands on the colour that is printed in the annexure.

The colour system is only honest if the base light is neutral. That is the whole reason the brand's warm-zone law gives way here, and it is why the variance is worth recording rather than hiding.

The ruling Issue 01 · 2026-10-20 ·  24 / 61

Read the minimum column

Uniformity 0.47 at the pass is a 2.1:1 ratio across the most safety-critical surface in the store, where staff handle boiling water. It is inside the tolerance for a working kitchen, but it means the task light must be positioned rather than assumed.

Back of house at 166 lux average with 58.6 at the worst point is below the level most commercial kitchens design to. This pack records it, names it, and specifies a remedy that does not alter Ryan's design — §04.5.

The number that makes it comparable

56 076 lumens installed, 50 468 lumens maintained at his light-loss factor of 0.900, over 45 m² of floor — roughly 1 120 maintained lumens per square metre for 15.5 W/m². High for a retail unit, and correct for a food-preparation space that also has to read as a lit white box from the mall concourse.

04.4The 6 000 K variance, recorded

The Brand Manual sets warm light by zone. This store is 6 000 K throughout. That is a variance, and a variance written down with a reason, a date and an owner is a decision — the same variance left unwritten is a defect found at audit.

FieldRecord
VarianceV-01 · Lighting colour temperature, all zones
Brand law variedBrand Manual V2.0, Part 7 "Light as Material": zone colour temperatures (warm at pass, ordering and seating)
Design installed6 000 K throughout, per ACDC calculation dated 2026-10-05
ReasonA neutral base is the only base on which a chosen colourway reads as itself. Warm light tints blue towards grey-green and lime towards yellow, so the store would show an approximation of the colour the franchisee bought.
Approved byRicardo Maio, principal — ruling of 2026-10-20
OwnerDesign authority, with ACDC as lighting authority
ReviewAt next brand manual revision, or on any change to the colour system

What the variance does not license

  • It does not relax the neon rule. One neon per surface, 12% maximum, and the no-nightclub test still applies — see §05.3.
  • It does not permit RGB as base lighting. The base is white at 6 000 K; colour is a wash laid over it and never a substitute for it.
  • It does not travel to print. Packaging, menu boards, comms and the annexure stay on the brand's own palette and proportion.

Why record it at all

Because in three years someone will measure 6 000 K against a manual that says 2 700 K and conclude the store was built wrong. This page is the answer: it was built wrong on purpose, by the principal, on this date, for this reason.

04.5The two areas the calculation does not cover

One area is calculated and too dark at its worst point. One area is not calculated at all. Neither is a design failure — both are the edge of the source, and the pack's job is to publish the edge rather than pretend it is not there.

Gap 1 · Back of house — 166 lux average, 58.6 lux minimum

Back of house is where staff carry boiling water across a wet floor with knives within reach. An office corridor is lit to about 100 lux; a commercial kitchen is normally designed to 300–500. The average is defensible for a small prep room. The 58.6 lux patch is the one that matters, because it is exactly where a fitting's distribution falls away and where a person steps backwards.

The pack's remedy, which does not alter Ryan's design: add one surface-mounted linear fitting of the same family and colour temperature over the wash-up and the circulation path, on the same circuit and the same driver type, commissioned to the same scene. It is an addition to a schedule, not a redesign of one — and it is priced and approved as a variation before installation.

Gap 2 · The eat zone — never calculated

Ryan's six calculated areas cover sales, retail, ordering, the pass, the bowl dispenser and back of house. The seating area has no calculation — which, in a food court, is where the customer consumes the product they just bought.

The pack specifies 200 lux average, 120 lux minimum at the seat, warm-neutral at 6 000 K to match the rest of the room, with no fitting within 900 mm of a seated eye line. This value is authored by this pack, not calculated, and every document that prints it says so.

Status of both gaps — closed on instruction, recorded as risk

The principal has decided not to send these back to ACDC. So they are handled here rather than argued: Gap 1 by an additive fitting, Gap 2 by an authored design value. Both are carried in the risk register at §11.1 with an owner. A pack that quietly omits them is worse than one that prints them.

A lighting design is a promise until someone measures the room. These are the measurements that turn it into a fact, taken before the fitter is paid and before the store opens.

#CheckMethod and pass conditionWhen
L1Lux by zoneCalibrated meter, grid of nine points per territory at 0.85 m, compared to §04.2. Pass: average ≥ 90% of design, min ≥ 80% of design.Commissioning
L2UniformitySame grid. Pass: min/average ≥ 0.40 everywhere except the pass, ≥ 0.45.Commissioning

The commissioning rule

No lighting stage payment is released, and no store opens, until L1 to L7 are recorded on the same sheet, signed by the commissioning agent and countersigned by the franchisee. The sheet goes into the handover pack at §10.2 and a copy into the annexure's commissioning record.

L6 is the one item nobody will thank you for until the night it matters. It is not in Ryan's report; it is a statutory requirement on any premises the public enters, and a pack that leaves it implicit leaves it to whoever installs the distribution board.

05.1Two palettes, one proportion

The most common mistake in a franchise design pack is to apply the packaging colour rule to the room. They are the same rule, and they are opposite.

Brand layer — print, packaging, comms, menu boardsStore layer — walls, counters, ceiling, joinery
FieldBlack #000000 — 70%White RAL 9016 — 70%
CounterpartWhite knockout — 18%Black grounding — 18%
AccentLime or the store's colour — 12%The store's colour — 12%
WhyIt is read. Black makes lime and the crest legible at a glance.It is lit. White returns light, so the colourway reads at half the installed load.

The line to remember

The branding has black. The shop must be white. A store that copies the packaging looks like a box. A store that inverts it is a room the packaging was designed for.

What black still does in the store — the 18%

The floor. A white floor in a wet, floury, tomato-sauce environment is a maintenance decision, not a design one. Matte black, sealed, with a defined cleaning regime.

Shadow gaps and plinths. The 6 mm line where joinery meets wall is what makes white joinery read as designed rather than as flat boxes pushed together.

Kick plates and edge trims. Where a shoe hits, where a mop hits. Black hides what white would advertise by Tuesday.

The logo field. The crest is a black-ground mark. It sits on black, wherever it appears in the room.

Equipment. Cookers, fridges, canopy, the pass. Specified black where there is a choice; where there is not, the black trim around it does the work.

The datum line. White walls with no black line read as a clinic corridor. One horizontal black datum is the difference between a clinic and a restaurant.

05.3Lit or painted — the only cost distinction that matters

A store can carry its colour two ways. One costs an afternoon and no lost trade. The other costs days and a closed shop. The choice is the franchisee's, and they must make it knowing which is which.

LIT — delivered by the RGB layerPAINTED — delivered by the surface
HowNeutral white surface, colour added by light from a controlled channelThe surface itself is coloured: paint, laminate, powder coat, tile
Change laterAn afternoon. No closure, no builder, no messDays. Store closed. Trades on site
Change fromThe controller, or remotely from head officeA purchase order and a repaint
Best onWalls washed at grazing angle, niche backs, edge lines, ceiling coves, the sign fieldHigh-wear surfaces, anything in daylight, anything a customer touches
Fails whenThe surface is not neutral white, or the fitting is too far from the wallThe store changes hands, or the brand direction moves
CostsCapital in the controller and channel; near-zero to changeCapital in the finish; full re-cost to change

The rule for the annexure

Every coloured surface in the store is tagged LIT or PAINTED on page 3 of the annexure, with its territory and its area. A franchisee who wants to change colour later reads that page and knows, in one glance, whether they are buying an update or a closure.

What "lit" demands of the surface — and this is where fit-outs fail

A colour wash is only as good as the white it lands on. The surface must be neutral, cleanable and reflectance-tested: no yellowing, no warm cast, no visible texture that breaks the gradient. A warm or dirty white turns the franchisee's blue into grey-green and the store blames the light fitting, the colour, and eventually the brand.

What "painted" demands of the contract

A painted colour is a permanent decision recorded in a document, so it carries the three signatures at page 7 of the annexure. Nobody repaints a store on a verbal instruction, and nobody signs for a colour they were told about in a corridor.

05.4The RGB engine

The colourway is not a paint chip. It is a recipe: a white surface, a distance, an angle, a value, and a calibration. This page is what makes the same colour look the same in two stores built by two different contractors.

ParameterRequirementWhy it exists
Surface reflectance≥ 80% diffuse, neutral (no warm cast), matte at 5–10 gloss unitsReflectance sets how much colour you get per watt; a warm cast shifts every hue
Channel distance60–100 mm from the wall face, grazing; never > 150 mmToo close scallops the light; too far drops the intensity into a wash
Channel setbackRecessed so the diode is not visible from any customer eye lineA visible source reads as a strip light, not as colour
RGB valueThe store's hex converted to the controller's 0–255 channel, recorded on the annexureThe only way a fitter can set it without guessing
CalibrationMeasured at commissioning against a spectrometer reading, adjusted to within ΔE ≤ 3 of the annexure plateTwo factories, two batches, two colours — unless calibrated
Base lightWhite 6 000 K, always on, always underneath the colourColour is additive, never a substitute for illumination
Mix limitColour at ≤ 12% of any surface's visible area, and never the only light on a working surfaceThe manual's neon rule, and the no-nightclub test

What the engine may not do

It may not animate across a customer's face. It may not chase, pulse, strobe or respond to music. It may not be the base lighting of the store. It may not be the only illuminant in any territory. A colour system that becomes a light show has left the brand — and the audit test for this is one question: would a customer describe this store as "nightclub"? If yes, it is wrong.

Colour is the single most subjective thing on a construction site, and the single most likely thing to be argued about at handover. The engine exists so that the argument is settled by a number on a page rather than by whoever is standing in the room with the client.

05.5Control: one standard for the whole network

A colour system is only as good as its controller. If every store buys its own, the network has fifty systems and nobody can change anything from head office.

The standard, specified

ItemRequirement
ProtocolDALI-2 (IEC 62386) with DT8 colour control. An open international standard, so no franchise is locked to one supplier for twenty years, and one protocol drives both the 6 000 K base and the colour layer.
ControllerNetworked application controller per store, addressable from head office over the network. Pushes colour and scene updates without sending anyone to site.
Pixel surfacesDMX512-A / Art-Net gateway as an interface off the same controller — never a second system with its own brain.
CapacityMaximum control gear per line, minimum zone and scene count, and spare capacity for the next fit-out change — stated in the order, not discovered later.
Local overrideAt the counter, by staff, in one action. A system staff cannot control is a system they defeat with a plug.
FallbackNetwork loss falls back to a safe white scene. Not to darkness, and not to the last colour, at 19:00 on a Friday.
RecordOne address book and one commissioning record per store, held centrally.

S1 Open100%Store colour at 100% of its limitTrading

05.6What the annexure carries, and what it may not

Eight pages per store. The main pack holds every rule; the annexure holds one colour and no arguments.

PgPageContent
1CoverStore, territory code, colourway name, pack revision it was issued against
2Colourway plateThe colour at full bleed with hex, RGB channel value, and its triad — white field, black grounding, accent
3Surface mapEvery coloured surface, its territory, and whether it is LIT or PAINTED
4RGB recipePer lighting zone: channel value, intensity, calibration target, and the scene it belongs to
5Procurement cardWhat to order: product, reference, finish, quantity — no prices, no alternatives
6Signage and façadeThis store's sign artwork against the façade template, with the crest lockup and EST 2025
7Approval recordThree signatures: design authority, brand owner, franchisee — with date and pack revision
8Cross-referenceEvery annexure line mapped to the pack page that governs it; the reading map

Four things an annexure may never contain

  • A rule. Rules live in the pack, once. A rule in an annexure is a rule that will be revised in fifty places or none.
  • An alternative. The annexure states what to order, not what else would do.
  • A price. Prices change; documents are signed. A signed document with a price on it is a contract to that price.
  • A comparison to another store. The annexure is about this store, and a franchisee comparing their colour to someone else's is a dispute in draft.

The test of a good annexure

Hand it to a fitter who has never seen this store, with the main pack on the table. If they can order the colour, set the controller and hang the sign without asking a question, the annexure is finished. If they have to ask which page governs what, page 8 is not doing its job.

05.7Plate 03 — colour as light, in the room

This is the page a franchisee should look at longest. It is the difference between buying a colour and buying a colour system: the same blue, delivered three ways, on surfaces that can each be changed separately.

What this plate proves

The wall behind the counter is white. The blue you see is a strip in a channel, washing a neutral surface. Change the strip and the store is a different colour by the end of the afternoon, with the store open. That is the whole commercial argument for the lit colourway — and it is why the white field is a cost decision, not a taste one.

Where the colour must be painted instead — the tile wall, the fascia sign field — the annexure marks the surface PAINTED, and the change becomes a refit event. Two mechanisms, one colour, and the annexure tells the franchisee which is which before they choose.

06.1How to read a material line

A material line that only names a product is a suggestion. This is the anatomy of a line that can actually be ordered, priced and inspected.

FieldWhat it answersIf it is missing
ProductWhat it is, genericallyThe contractor substitutes on price
Manufacturer & referenceExactly which one was designed"Or similar" becomes "or cheaper"
Colour codeThe value, in the system it will be bought in — RAL, Pantone, or a manufacturer's own codeTwo batches, two colours, one argument
FinishMatte, satin, gloss; texture; sheen levelThe right colour in the wrong sheen reads as the wrong colour
Thickness / profileWhat it is dimensionallyJunctions close up 2–3 mm wrong everywhere
SubstrateWhat it is fixed to, and what that must beThe finish fails in six months and blames the cleaner
FixingAdhesive, mechanical, or both — and the methodSomeone invents one on the day
Sample statusWhether a physical sample must be approved before orderingThe first time anyone sees the colour is on the wall
Approved equivalentWhether an alternative is permitted, and what "equivalent" means hereAnything is equivalent if nobody defined it
Lead timeWeeks, from order to siteThe programme is written before anyone asks

The substitution rule

Where a line says "or approved equivalent", equivalent means: same colour value within ΔE ≤ 2, same or better wear class, same thickness tolerance, same fire rating, and a physical sample approved by the design authority before the order. Where a line says "no alternative", there is none — usually because the surface carries colour, and a different product takes the colour differently.

The rest of this section is written in that anatomy. Where a value was not supplied by the design authority, the line says "to be confirmed by sample" rather than inventing a reference — because a wrong reference in a pack is worse than an honest blank.

06.2Floor

The floor carries the grounding layer of the store — the 18% that stops a white room reading as a clinic — and it carries the only walk-over electrical element in the fit-out.

ItemSpecification
F-01 Floor finishMatte black, seamless resin or large-format porcelain, sealed. Slip rating R10 minimum in customer areas, R11 at the pass and wash-up. No polished finish anywhere a customer walks with a tray.
ColourBlack, matte. Must read as one continuous plane — no visible tile grid in the customer field. Reference to be confirmed by sample.
SubstrateLandlord's structural slab, levelled to ±3 mm over 3 m. Fall to drain verified before screed — see H1.
FixingAdhesive or screed per manufacturer; movement joints at doorways and at every 6 m, aligned with the setting-out grid, not placed where they look tidy.
F-02 Walk-over RGBIP67 walk-over linear LED, recessed with a flush trim. Stainless or anodised housing, sealed cable entry, driver off the floor in an accessible location. Two runs, set out to the circulation line, not to the shell.
F-02 accessEach run must be replaceable from above without lifting the floor. A walk-over strip with no access is a permanent black scar the day it fails.
F-03 Floor text"Order & Pick Up Here" — produced as a robust inlay or a cut vinyl under a sacrificial clear coat, not as paint. Must survive mopping, trolleys and a commercial cleaning regime.
Approved alternativePermitted: porcelain in place of resin, or resin in place of porcelain, if slip rating, mattness and seamlessness are matched and a sample is approved. Not permitted: a lighter floor, or a gloss finish.

The maintenance truth about a black floor

Black shows every crumb and every scuff of flour in a way a grey floor does not. That is the cost of the grounding, and it is a cleaning regime rather than a design defect. It is stated here so that it is priced into the franchisee's operating model rather than discovered in week two.

06.3Walls and ceiling

The white field, and the one wall that carries the colour. Everything here exists to give the RGB layer a neutral, even, cleanable surface — or to be the surface that is coloured for good.

ItemSpecification
W-01 White wallNeutral white, ≥ 80% diffuse reflectance, matte 5–10 gloss units, scrubbable and wipeable. RAL 9016 reference. No warm cast — a warm white turns the store's blue grey-green.
W-01 substrateMoisture-resistant board, taped and skimmed to a class-2 finish. Any texture in the substrate telegraphs through a matte white under grazing light.
W-02 Tile wallGlazed subway tile, elongated format, running bond, white grout, 2 mm joints. Set out centred on the pass opening; no cut below 60 mm. Carries the store's colour in the tile body, not in a painted line.
W-03 Colour panelsThe store's accent colour as flat panels, on the 12%. Painted or faced; see the annexure for which. Panels are removable for access and replaceable without disturbing the wall.
W-04 Niche and shelvingRecessed niches with white floating shelves and a colour LED under-strip. Rebate depth set so the shelf shadow is a line, not a smudge. Service access behind each niche.
C-01 CeilingMatte white, demountable where services sit above, plasterboard elsewhere. Recessed linear luminaires flush, aligned to the counter line — never to the shell.
C-02 Coves and channelsRecessed channels as drawn, with a shadow detail at the ceiling junction. No surface-mounted trunking in any customer-facing area.
Approved alternativeWalls: a scrubbable vinyl wall covering permitted where a plaster finish would not survive, if reflectance and neutrality are proven by sample. Tile: no alternative — the running bond and the elongated format are the design. Ceiling: a metal tile grid permitted in back of house only.

The white-surface risk, stated plainly

White shows every mark in a wet, floury kitchen. That is the real cost of the white ruling. The pack answers it with specification rather than optimism: scrubbable finishes, sacrificial panels behind the cook line, a replaceable dado, and a touch-up kit in the handover. A store that looks tired at month six is a specification failure, not a white failure.

06.4Counters and tops

The counter is the store. It is the surface the customer leans on, the surface the food is handed across, and the surface that carries three of the store's four colour elements at once.

ItemSpecification
K-01 Service topEezi Quartz solid surface, 20 mm, white. Coved upstand where it meets the tiled wall. Joints inconspicuous, never within 300 mm of the pass opening.
K-02 Eating counterThermoformed white acrylic, 1 100 mm high, seamless radius front. The one place where the customer physically touches the design. Impact-resistant grade, replaceable panels.

Why the counter tolerances are tighter than the walls

Everything a customer touches gets inspected at 400 mm, and everything they merely see gets inspected at two metres. That is why the counter carries a ±2 mm level tolerance and the wall carries ±3 mm over three metres: the tolerance follows the viewing distance, not the trade.

J-04 Wet areaFull-height impervious finish to 2 100 mm at wash-up and pasta cooking. Sealed junctions, no silicone-only corners. Floor fall and drain access maintained.
J-05 Service accessEvery driver, valve, isolator and controller reachable without demolishing a panel. Access panels are hinged or magnetic, and are recorded on a plan in the handover pack.
J-06 Waste and storageBins off the customer path, ventilated, on a washable base. The staff route from pass to waste never crosses the customer route.

07.1Counter build-up, layer by layer

Read from the floor up. Each layer assumes the one below it is finished and within tolerance — which is why the sequence matters as much as the specification.

LLayerBuildDim.
1FloorFinished black floor, level and sealed. The counter sits on the finished floor, not on screed.± 3 / 3 m
2PlinthRecessed black plinth, set back from the counter face so the toe line reads as a shadow.set back 60 mm
3Kick LEDColour strip recessed above the plinth, in an aluminium channel with a diffuser, driven from an accessible driver.set back 25 mm
4Base carcass18 mm MR MDF, sealed, on adjustable feet; levelled and locked before any front is fitted.18 mm
5Counter frontColour-faced panel, 6 mm shadow gap to the floor and to the wall; removable on clips for access.gap 6 mm
6Structural topSub-top in moisture-resistant board to carry the working surface and its loads.18 mm
7Working surfaceEezi Quartz, 20 mm, white; joints inconspicuous; coved upstand at the wall.20 mm
8Eating counterThermoformed white acrylic at 1 100 mm, radius front, mechanically fixed to the sub-top, not glued only.1 100 mm
9Edge and shadowBlack edge trim where the top oversails; the 6 mm line continues around every visible return.6 mm ± 1

The access rule for this detail

Layers 3, 5 and 7 must each be removable without disturbing the other two. A driver behind a sealed counter front is a counter front that gets cut open with a multi-tool at 11 p.m., and the repair is visible for the life of the store.

This detail is the pack's own work. It is not on the drawing set — the drawings show the counter as an intent, not as a build-up. Where the pack and the drawing disagree about a dimension, the drawing wins; where the drawing is silent about a layer, this page governs.

07.2RGB integration

The colour layer is a building element, not an accessory. It has a substrate, a channel, a driver, a cable route and an access hatch — and if any one of those is missing, the colour is a strip of tape that fails in a year.

LElementRequirement
1SubstrateNeutral white, matte, reflectance ≥ 80%, free of texture that would break the gradient. This is the layer that decides the colour, and it is the one everyone skips.
2ChannelRecessed aluminium profile with a diffuser, set 60–100 mm off the wall face at a grazing angle. Never surface-mounted in a customer-facing area.
3Tape / moduleColour-controlled, CRI-matched to the base, 24 V, sealed to IP44 minimum (IP65 in the wet zone). Batch recorded on the commissioning sheet.
4DriverDALI-2 DT8, one per zone or per group as drawn, sited in an accessible ceiling void or cupboard — not above a fixed ceiling with no hatch.
5Cable routeSegregated from mains, mechanically protected, with a service loop at every joint so a module can be replaced without cutting the run.
6AddressingEvery zone addressed to the territory code (CT-…) and logged in the store's address book. An unaddressed zone is a zone nobody can fix remotely.
7CommissioningSpectrometer reading at the wall, adjusted to ΔE ≤ 3 against the annexure plate; scene recall tested for all seven scenes.

The three failures this detail prevents

  • The visible diode. A strip you can see is a strip the customer reads as a light, not as colour — and the 12% rule is immediately breached in perception even if it is obeyed in area.
  • The dead run. No access, no service loop, no replacement: one failed module takes out three metres of the store's colour until the next refit.
  • The drifting zone. Two drivers on two batches, uncalibrated, show as two different blues on one wall — and the franchisee concludes the design is wrong.

07.3Junctions and setting out

Bad buildings are not built of bad materials. They are built at the joins. These are the five that decide how the store reads at 400 mm.

JunctionBuildTolerance
Floor to wallBlack floor runs to a 6 mm shadow line at the wall base, not a skirting. Skirting in a wet food area is a trap for water and dirt.6 ± 1 mm
Wall to ceilingShadow gap detail at the ceiling junction; the ceiling plane floats above the wall rather than butting it.6 ± 1 mm
Tile to paintTile terminates on a purpose-made trim, not a bead of sealant. The trim line is set out on the grid, level, and reads as deliberate.± 1 mm
Counter to wallCoved upstand, then a 6 mm shadow gap where the counter meets a painted wall. Both details on the same counter, because the quartz and the paint behave differently.6 ± 1 mm
Niche to wallRebate formed before tiling, not cut after. Shelf sits in the rebate; LED under-strip hidden behind the shelf nose.± 1 mm

Tile setting out — the rule that saves the wall

Set out from the centre of the pass opening, not from a corner. Cuts land at the least visible end, no cut is narrower than 60 mm, and the bond runs horizontally to the counter line. On an elongated subway format, a 20 mm cut at a corner is the difference between a designer's wall and a tiler's wall — and it is decided in ten minutes with a chalk line before the first tile is fixed, or not at all.

Setting out is a design act

Every one of these junctions was decided at a drawing board. A fitter who "makes it work" on site is not being pragmatic — they are making a design decision that nobody will record, on a surface that will be photographed for the next ten years.

07.4The wet pass, and fixing to a shopfront you do not own

The two hardest interfaces in the unit: the wettest place in the store, and the one surface the tenant must not touch.

The pass — built for a hose, not a cloth

RequirementDetail
Impervious to 2 100 mmFull-height tile, sealed junctions, no plasterboard within splash reach
Floor fallFall to drain maintained through the finished floor; no ponding anywhere at handover, tested with a bucket
Coved cornersCoved where floor meets wall at the wash-up; silicone alone is a mould line within a season
IP65All fittings in the wash-up zone; drivers outside the wet envelope
Equipment isolationEvery appliance isolatable without moving it; isolators labelled and recorded
VentilationExtract sized by the mechanical contractor; the pack states the canopy position and the make-up air path only

The shopfront — landlord-owned, and this is where programmes die

The shopfront, the fascia and the sightline are the landlord's, not the tenant's. The signage is an independently mounted illuminated 3D logo, whose fixing method, weight, projection and power supply are not specified on the drawing set — a genuine gap, recorded here rather than papered over.

Hold point H4 — before signage fabrication

The signage cannot be fabricated until four things exist in writing: the landlord's written consent to the fixing method, a structural check of what the logo is fixed to, the municipal signage approval, and the electrical supply point confirmed. Fabricating before these is the single most expensive common mistake in mall fit-outs: a sign made, a landlord who says no, and a store that opens behind a blank fascia.

The two artwork corrections carried on every store

The rendered signage shows EST. 2023 and "Unusual Pasta Attitude". Brand law freezes the crest at EST 2025 and the line as "LEVEL UP YOUR HUNGER". Both are corrected on the annexure's signage page for every store, and no signage order is released on uncorrected artwork.

08.2Plate 04 — the mark that may not change

The shopfront may change colour. This may not change at all. The crest is the one element in the entire fit-out that is identical in every store on earth, and it is the first thing an auditor checks.

Fixed foreverWhat "fixed" actually means on site
Crest anatomyShield, forks, knot, and their relative sizes. No redraw, no simplification, no "cleaner" version from a signwriter.
EST 2025The year on the crest. The renders show EST. 2023 — that is a render error, not an option.
Brand line"LEVEL UP YOUR HUNGER" — once, in its fixed position. The renders' "Unusual Pasta Attitude" is not a brand line.
Wordmark typePAPA PASTA in the supplied lockup. Never re-set in another weight, never outlined by a fabricator.
Clear spaceThe exclusion zone travels with the lockup, scaled proportionally to the fascia.

The fabricator rule

Artwork files are released as supplied, never redrawn. A signwriter who "tidies up" a crest produces a shopfront that fails brand audit and has to be remade at the franchisee's cost — and the remake is not covered by anyone's warranty.

08.3Approval, per store

Because the façade now changes with the colour, signage approval is a per-store event. That is a real change in process, and the risk it creates is a store fitted, lit and stocked behind a blank fascia while a consent sits in someone's inbox.

#ApprovalWhoTrigger — when it must start
A1Colourway on the network menuBrand ownerAt annexure issue, page 2
A2Sign artwork and lockupBrand ownerAt annexure issue, page 6
A3Landlord design reviewLandlordBefore fabrication — typically 4–6 weeks
A4Municipal signage approvalLocal authorityBefore fabrication — typically 6–10 weeks
A5Structural consent to fixingLandlord's engineerBefore fabrication — H4
A6Illumination and light-trespass checkLandlord / authorityWith A3, using the lit façade sample

The programme consequence, stated for the franchisee

A3 and A4 are the two longest external approvals in the project and they start after the colour is chosen, not before. Choosing a colourway late does not delay the colour — it delays the sign, and therefore the opening. Annexure first, then fit-out. That single sequencing rule is worth more to the programme than any trade acceleration.

What the annexure must prove before A3 is lodged

  • The colour is on the network menu, at the value printed — no "similar to".
  • The crest is unaltered: anatomy, EST 2025, and the fixed tagline.
  • The illumination is even, with no visible source, and the lit sample has been photographed at night, not rendered.
  • The sign is independently mounted, and nothing is fixed to the landlord's shopfront glass or frame.

09.3Who pays for what

This pack quotes no price. A price belongs to a site, a date and a quantity surveyor. What the pack does instead is more durable: it separates the lines a franchisee pays for from the lines somebody else owns.

Scope lineWho pays What this pack fixes
Shell and shopfrontLandlord 8 040 × 5 600 mm with a 3 600 mm ceiling datum. No fixing into the shopfront without written consent — §07.4.
Services to the tenancyLandlord to the point of supply Power, water, waste and the isolator to the tenancy boundary. Everything inside is the tenant's — §09.1.
Design and artworkHead office The plate value, crest, wordmark, wayfinding template and the fourteen essentials — §05.2, §08.1. Never charged to a store.
Fit-outFranchisee Counters, joinery, finishes, ceiling, lighting supply and install, signage fabrication, commissioning — §06, §07, §08.
LightingFranchisee Twenty fittings, 698 W, 6 000 K, one schedule — §04.3. The quantity is not negotiable; the mounting is what a site argues about.
Signage consentFranchisee, approved by the brand The design is head office's; the application and the mall's consent are the store's. The longest lead in the pack — §08.3, §09.2.
Controller and networkFranchisee Bought to the head-office standard — DALI-2 with DT8 colour control, local override, safe scene on network loss — §05.5. Not to the fitter's preference.
Proof and commissioningFranchisee Paid for by the store, witnessed against §04.6 and §10.2. A store that opens without it has no record that it was built right.

What is deliberately absent. No rate, no total, no supplier quotation and no allowance. A quantity surveyor prices this pack line by line against §06 and §07. The annexure carries no money at all — so a store can re-tender without re-issuing its colour, and a price change never re-opens a signed document.

What a franchisee signs, then, is a scope and a specification — never a sum. The sum arrives from a tender, and it is priced against this document, not against a conversation.

09.4The five decisions that move the total

Nearly every fit-out overrun in this network will trace back to one of these five. They are not the five biggest lines — a lighting schedule is a known quantity. They are the five where a decision made late costs more than the same decision made well.

1 · Signage

The only line that needs a third party's consent, and it sits on the opening date. A rejected application does not cost money as much as it costs weeks — a store that cannot trade is paying rent on a finished shop.

LEVER — start the application at annexure issue, not at handover · §08.3

2 · The counter run

Solid surface, carcass, fronts, shadow gaps and the services chase all scale with millimetres of run rather than with the room. A change after the carcasses are cut is not a variation, it is a rebuild — and the top is re-made, not adjusted.

LEVER — decide the run once against the drawing, then freeze it · §03.5

3 · Lit or painted

Every coloured surface is one or the other. Lit costs more to install and far less to change; painted is the reverse. Paint a surface that was always going to move and you close the store to change a colour. Light one that will never move and you bought a controller you do not use.

LEVER — lit where it will move, painted where it will not · annexure page 3

4 · Tiling

Area, substrate preparation and grout colour are three separately priced lines, and the metro tile arrives in a fixed format. Tiled from the middle and you cut at both corners, where the eye goes first — and the visible wall becomes the one that looks cheap.

LEVER — full tile at the visible corner, cut at the ceiling · §06.3

5 · Changes after sign-off

Every variation after the annexure is signed re-opens three documents: the shop drawing, the procurement card and the approval record. The colour, the light and the record drift apart, and the store is judged against an annexure that no longer describes it.

LEVER — one review, before signature · §10.1

The cheapest decision in this pack is the review before signature. It costs one conversation, and it is the only point at which all three documents can still be changed together. After that the annexure is a record, not a proposal.

10.2Commissioning and the handover pack

Handover is not a set of keys. It is the set of documents that let the next person operate, maintain and repair the store without the people who built it.

#In the handover packWhat it lets someone do
1Signed main pack and annexureKnow what was agreed, against which revision
2L1–L7 commissioning sheetProve the lighting performs, and re-measure it later
3Scene and address bookRecall, change and diagnose every lighting zone
4As-built drawingsFind what is behind a panel before drilling it
5Service access planReach every driver, valve and isolator
6Approved sample boardMatch a repair in five years, not by eye
7Touch-up kit and spare modulesFix the small things before they become refits
8Cleaning and maintenance regimeKeep white surfaces white, and the colour true
9Supplier list with referencesReorder the exact product, not a lookalike
10Approvals register, closedDemonstrate compliance on demand
11Warranty scheduleKnow what is covered, by whom, until when
12Defects and snag list, signed offClose the contract, not just the job

The three tests at handover

  • Look up. Is the ceiling line straight, is every fitting in its channel, is there a visible diode anywhere?
  • Look down. Does the floor read as one plane, are the walk-over strips flush, is there a shadow line at the wall base?
  • Look at the colour. Set S1, walk the store, and compare the wall to the annexure plate in daylight and again at night. If it is not the same colour, commissioning is not finished.

Snagging is not the last ten per cent of the work. It is the ten per cent the customer sees every day for the next ten years.

11.2Revision control and colophon

The pack is a controlled document. This page is how a store built in three years' time is judged against the rules that existed when it was approved.

ControlRule
Revision numberingWhole numbers only. Rev 02 supersedes Rev 01 in full; there are no partial revisions and no page-level substitutes.
Who may reviseThe design authority, with lighting changes countersigned by ACDC and colour changes by the brand owner.
How a store is judgedAgainst the revision printed on its signed annexure page 7 — never against the current revision. A store cannot be failed for a rule that did not exist when it was built.
Annexure couplingEvery annexure prints the pack revision it was issued against. A new pack revision does not invalidate existing annexures; it invalidates only their future reissues.
WithdrawalAn annexure found contradicting the pack is withdrawn and reissued. The pack is never edited to match an annexure.
DistributionFranchise network and approved suppliers only. Superseded revisions are archived, not deleted.
